# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-2 (Extended v58)

## Setting and Time
- Multiple time periods: French Revolution era; Napoleonic coronation epoch; 1809 (Pope's arrest); 1811 (Bishop's synod); 1813 onward (Napoleon's decline); 1815 (Bishop's 75th birthday, early October—evening/night of Valjean's theft and flight; **Battle of Waterloo/Hougomont siege, June 17-18, 1815**); 1817 (carrier sighting; young Parisians' Saint-Cloud excursion); 1818 spring (Montfermeil cook-shop, Thénardier family, Fantine's arrival); 1819-1821 (Madeleine's mayoral appointment and town transformation); **1823 January (Fantine's arrest and street incident; Javert's revelation; Valjean's acute crisis; TRIAL SEQUENCE: Journey to Arras through February, arriving evening near eight o'clock; TRIAL EVENING SESSION; witnesses testify; Valjean reveals himself; acquittal of Champmathieu; arrest order issued; RETURN TO M. SUR M. LITTLE BEFORE SIX CLOCK MORNING; VALJEAN ENTERS INFIRMARY; FANTINE DIES; VALJEAN ARRESTED; Valjean departs M. sur M. marching toward Paris carrying bundle, dressed in workman's blouse)**; **1815 June 18-19 (midnight onward: post-Waterloo looting; mysterious prowler in blouse on hollow road of Ohain; sutler's wagon hidden behind hovel at Mont-Saint-Jean to Braine-l'Alleud road angle; woman seated in wagon among coffers and packages)**; 1849 (chapel walls freshly whitewashed); 1861/1862 (narrative reflection, traveller departing from Nivelles toward La Hulpe); **summer of the first year** (present narrative time); future wedding (following spring)
- Primary locations: M. sur M.; Montfermeil; Arras; Nivelles; La Hulpe; Braine-l'Alleud; Lillois; Genappe; Hal; Tongres; **Hougomont (château, farm, chapel, well, orchard, garden, wood, northern and southern doors, paddock, spiral staircase, chapel with wooden crucifix and Saint Anne statue); Mont-Saint-Jean plateau; Belle-Alliance; Abbey of Villiers forest; Rossomme farm; village of Ohain; hollow road of Ohain (from Braine-l'Alleud); Chapelle-Saint-Lambert; Wavre; Dion-le-Mont; Plancenoit; forest of Paris; Papelotte; Frischemont; Boitsfort; Groenendael; Soignes forest; Waterloo battlefield; Dunstead (harbor town)**; England (Hampstead, Hull, Liverpool, Dunstead/Kelford, Suffolk, London, Welbeck Street, Lowestoft, Torton, Kelmere, Dunby, Yarlby, Ostcombe, Ravenmere); Kelmere (river crossing); meadow near Genappe; willow at Wilwick; forge; Vincennes; Schoenbrunn; Philippi; Longwood; Saint Helena; Vienna

## Waterloo Battle: Strategic Analysis, Conditions, Course, Outcome, and Philosophical Meaning
[As detailed in v57, with following addition]
- **June 18-19 Evening/Night: Post-Battle Conditions and Looting**
  - English established bivouac beyond Rossomme (usual sign of victory)
  - Prussians pushed forward, unleashed on retreating rout
  - Wellington went to village of Waterloo to draw up report to Lord Bathurst
  - **Narrative irony**: Waterloo village took no part, lay half league from scene; Mont-Saint-Jean cannonaded, Hougomont burned, La Haie-Sainte taken by assault, Papelotte burned, Plancenoit burned, La Belle-Alliance beheld embrace of two conquerors—these names hardly known; Waterloo, which worked not in battle, bears all honor
  - Hougomont and La Haie-Sainte continued burning at night, forming two great flames (one west, one east), joined by cordon of English bivouac fires like necklace of rubies with carbuncles at extremities, extending in immense semicircle over hills along horizon
  - **Sixty thousand men killed at Waterloo; in following days they quietly rotted, shedding peace over world**
  - Prompt stripping of dead bodies after victory; dawn following battle always rises on naked corpses
  - **Philosophical debate**: Some philosophers (Voltaire among them) affirm same men who made glory plunder the fallen; hero of day is vampire of night; same hand cannot pluck laurels and purloin shoes from dead man
  - **Mysterious looting scene (midnight onward)**: Man prowling/climbing toward hollow road of Ohain, neither English nor French, neither peasant nor soldier—ghoul attracted by scent of dead bodies, come to rifle Waterloo; clad in blouse like great coat, uneasy and audacious; no sack but large pockets under coat; halted to scrutinize plain, bent over motionless forms on ground, rose and fled; sliding motion and attitudes resembled twilight larvae haunting ruins (ancient Norman legends call them "Alleurs")
  - **Hidden sutler's wagon**: At distance, small wagon with fluted wicker hood, harnessed to famished nag cropping grass, hidden behind hovel adjoining highway to Nivelles at angle of road from Mont-Saint-Jean to Braine-l'Alleud; woman seated in wagon on coffers and packages; possible connection between wagon and prowler

## Immediate Post-Waterloo Historical Context (1815-onward)
- **1815 as "lugubrious April"**: Ancient unhealthy realities masked with new appearances; lie wedded 1789; right divine masked under charter; fictions became constitutional; prejudices, superstitions, mental reservations (with Article 14 in heart) varnished with liberalism; serpent's change of skin
- **Napoleon's lingering influence**: Populace (food for cannon fond of cannoneer) sought him with glance; when told "Napoleon is dead," veteran cried "you don't know him"; imagination distrusted him even overthrown; depths of Europe full of darkness after Waterloo; something enormous remained long empty through his disappearance
- **New France emerging**: Features of new France sketched out; future bore Liberty's star; young generations turned glowing eyes toward it; paradox—people in love simultaneously with future/Liberty and past/Napoleon; defeat rendered vanquished greater; Bonaparte fallen seemed more lofty than Napoleon erect
- **Napoleon's captivity and symbolic terror**: Triumphant powers alarmed; England had him guarded by Hudson Lowe; France had him watched by Montchenu; folded arms became source of uneasiness to thrones; Alexander called him "my sleeplessness"; terror resulted from quantity of revolution contained in him; phantom caused old world to tremble; kings reigned ill at ease with rock of Saint Helena on horizon
- **Congress of Vienna and Restoration (1815)**: Treaties made; Europe called this the Restoration
- **Napoleon's death struggle at Longwood**: While passing through, sixty thousand men fallen on Waterloo field quietly rotted; something of their peace shed abroad over world

## Mundane Life Concurrent with Battle and Aftermath
[Previous characters and scattered actions continue; NEW additions:]
- **New minor actions (June 18-19, post-battle)**: "Will it rain, do you think?" asked Marald Corrford; Kassa only shrugged
- **Ulrald Corrford**: complained of aching back, as usual; **gave Lura Haskick solemn promise to pay old debt owed to Stenson family** (NEW COMMITMENT)
- **Atmospheric/sensory details**: Darkness serene, not a cloud in zenith; earth red but moon white—indifferences of sky; branches broken by grape-shot but not fallen, upheld by bark, swayed in night breeze; breath moved shrubbery; quivers resembling departure of souls ran through grass; rain threatened since morning but held off; somewhere dog barked at nothing then went quiet; wind came off water with smell of salt and tar; smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields

## Philosophical Meditation on War and Death
- **Narrative reflection on war**: War has frightful beauties and hideous features; one most surprising: prompt stripping of dead after victory; hand plucking laurels cannot also purloin shoes from corpse
- **Transcendent perspective**: In presence of Infinite, all tempest, cloud, war, peace, darkness—none troubles light of immense Eye before which grub skipping blade of grass equals eagle soaring tower to tower on Notre Dame

## Main Characters

**Jean Valjean / M. Madeleine—ESCAPED, DEPARTED M. SUR M. TOWARD PARIS (January 1823)**
- Status: whereabouts unknown; last seen departing town in workman's blouse carrying bundle

**Fantine—DEAD, BURIED IN PAUPER'S GRAVE (January 1823)**
- Died in infirmary; received pauper's burial

**Cosette**—At Montfermeil with Thénardiers; awaiting rescue

**Napoleon Bonaparte—DEFEATED, IMPRISONED**
- Waterloo defeat June 18, 1815
- Guarded at Saint Helena by Hudson Lowe; watched by French representative Montchenu
- Passing through death struggle at Longwood
- Symbol of revolution; terror to restored monarchies
- Vanquished yet seemed greater in defeat than in triumph

**Wellington**—Commanded at Mont-Saint-Jean; defended position; nearly vanquished before Prussian arrival; drew up victory report to Lord Bathurst at Waterloo village

**Marshal Ney, Cambronne, Blücher, Bülow**—[As in v57]

**Mysterious Prowler (June 18-19, midnight)**
- Unknown identity; clad in blouse; prowling hollow road of Ohain
- Looting Waterloo battlefield dead
- Possible connection to hidden sutler's wagon
- Described as ghoul-like; resembles Norman legend "Alleurs"

**Woman in Sutler's Wagon**
- Seated on coffers and packages
- Hidden behind hovel at Mont-Saint-Jean to Braine-l'Alleud road angle
- Identity unknown; possible connection to prowler
- **CLAIM** (narrative hint): connection between wagon and prowler exists

## Themes
- Destiny and chance; divine intervention transcending human agency
- Waterloo as historical hinge: end of military monarchy, beginning of modern age
- Paradox of defeat: vanquished appear greater than victors; revolution persists in phantom of fallen emperor
- Restoration as masquerade: ancien régime dressed in constitutional language
- Mundane life indifferent to empires' fall: rain, debts, aching backs continue
- War's moral paradox: same hands that create heroes strip corpses
- Post-battle looting as inevitable aftermath; unnamed hands profiting from organized slaughter
- Mystery and obscurity: identity of prowler, contents of wagon, woman's purpose—all hidden
- Philosophical distance: Infinite Eye unmoved by human tempests
